verdict.summary:
LEGAL ANSWER — Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), regulation 4(1): the 48-hour average and the route out of it

1. THE LIMIT — 48 HOURS

Regulation 4(1) (text as originally made, and reproduced verbatim in the 'latest available (revised)' version supplied):

"Subject to regulation 5, a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days."

In the amended text the opening words are replaced by: "Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work, ...".

Answer to ask 1: the limit is an average of 48 hours for each seven days.

Four features of the limit matter and are routinely got wrong:

(a) It is an average, not a weekly ceiling. A worker may lawfully work more than 48 hours in a given week provided that, averaged across the applicable reference period, working time does not exceed 48 hours per seven days. Nothing in regulation 4 makes any single week a breach.

(b) Overtime counts. The words "including overtime" are express. A worker contracted for 40 hours can therefore average no more than 8 hours' overtime per week across the reference period before the limit is exceeded; there is no carve-out for voluntary, occasional or premium-paid overtime.

(c) The averaging window. Regulation 4(3): subject to paragraphs (4) and (5) and to any agreement under regulation 23(b), the reference period is (a) where a relevant agreement provides for successive periods of 17 weeks, each such period, or (b) otherwise, any period of 17 weeks in the course of employment. Regulation 4(4): where the worker has been employed for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period since he started work. Regulation 4(5): for a worker excluded from certain provisions by regulation 21, '17 weeks' is read as '26 weeks'. The 26-week figure changes the averaging window only — the 48-hour limit is unchanged.

(d) The averaging formula and excluded days. Regulation 4(6): average weekly working time = (A + B) / C, where A is aggregate working hours in the reference period, B is aggregate working hours in the period immediately after the reference period ending when the number of days worked equals the number of excluded days in the reference period, and C is the number of weeks in the reference period. Regulation 4(7) defines 'excluded days' as days in annual leave under regulation 13 (as amended, also 13A and 15B), sick leave, maternity (as amended, also paternity, adoption and parental) leave, and any period in respect of which the regulation 4(1) limit did not apply by reason of the worker's written agreement.

The employer's duty is in regulation 4(2): to take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect health and safety, to ensure the limit is complied with for each worker to whom it applies; and, as amended, to keep up-to-date records of all workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because the employer has obtained the worker's written agreement.

2. HOW A WORKER MAY BE TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT — THE INDIVIDUAL WRITTEN OPT-OUT (REGULATION 5(1))

Mechanism: the worker agrees with the employer in writing that the limit shall not apply in his case. Regulation 5(1):

"The limit specified in regulation 4(1) shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with his employer in writing that it should not apply in his case, provided that the employer complies with the requirements of paragraph (4)."

Regulation 5(2) and (3) supply the terms of that agreement:

- Duration — regulation 5(2)(a): the agreement may relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely.
- Withdrawal by the worker — regulation 5(2)(b): subject to any provision in the agreement for a different period of notice, it is terminable by the worker by giving not less than seven days' notice to the employer in writing.
- Cap on agreed notice — regulation 5(3): where the agreement provides for termination after a period of notice, that notice period must not exceed three months.

The amended regulation 4(1) adds a timing condition: the employer must have "first obtained" the worker's written agreement to perform such work — i.e. the opt-out must be in place before the worker performs working time that would otherwise breach the 48-hour average, not ratified afterwards.

Conditions and consequences in practice:

1. Writing. The agreement must be in writing and must be an agreement that the regulation 4(1) limit is not to apply. A written contract term can serve, provided it is a genuine agreement to disapply the limit and not merely an acknowledgment that long hours may occur.

2. Timing. Obtain the agreement before the work exceeding the limit is performed (regulation 4(1) as amended, "first obtained").

3. Records. The employer must keep up-to-date records of every worker carrying out work to which the limit does not apply by reason of such an agreement (regulation 4(2) as amended), and must comply with regulation 5(4) (the paragraph is cross-referenced in regulation 5(1); see verification note V3 below before relying on its detail).

4. Withdrawal. The worker may terminate the agreement on not less than seven days' written notice, unless the agreement provides a different notice period, which cannot exceed three months. On termination the 48-hour average applies again from that point; the employer must then schedule within the limit.

5. Effect is narrow. The opt-out disapplies regulation 4(1) only. It does not disapply the night-work limits (regulation 6), the rest period and break entitlements (regulations 10-12), the 48-hour weekly rest entitlement (regulation 11), the annual leave entitlement, or the employer's health-and-safety duty under regulation 4(2) in respect of workers to whom the limit still applies.

6. Not a contractual entitlement to work long hours. The opt-out removes a regulatory ceiling; it does not oblige the employer to offer, or the worker to accept, overtime.

3. OTHER ROUTES THAT ARE DISTINCT FROM THE REGULATION 5 OPT-OUT (flagged for verification — see V4)

These exist but must not be conflated with the opt-out:

- Unmeasured working time (regulation 19): where, because of the specific characteristics of the work, the duration of working time is not measured or predetermined, or can be determined by the worker himself (the paradigm case being managing executives and similar autonomous workers), specified provisions — understood to include regulation 4(1) and (2) — do not apply. This is a category exclusion, not an agreement.
- Workforce and collective agreements (regulation 23): regulation 4(3) is expressly subject to "any agreement under regulation 23(b)", which can modify the reference periods. This changes the averaging window, not the 48-hour figure.
- Regulation 21 workers: a 26-week reference period is substituted (regulation 4(5)); the worker remains within regulation 4, with a longer window.
- Part III exceptions generally: regulation 3 provides that Part II has effect subject to the exceptions in Part III, which cover specified sectors and worker categories (including seagoing and fisheries work). Workers excluded from the Regulations entirely fall outside regulation 4 altogether — a different proposition from opting out.
- Young workers: separate limits apply to young workers, and the regulation 5 opt-out is not the route by which those limits are varied. Verify the applicable provision (understood to be regulation 5A) before advising in any case involving a worker under 18.

4. VERSION AND VERIFICATION NOTES

V1. The 48-hour figure and the regulation 5(1) mechanism are quoted verbatim from the supplied sources and are identical in the as-made, 1998-10-01, 2003-08-01 and latest-available versions. The answer to both asks does not depend on which version is used.

V2. Reference period. The text supplied, including the "latest available (revised)" page, states 17 weeks in regulation 4(3). That same page lists a 01/01/2024 amendment among the versions of section 4. Before advising on the averaging window for any period on or after 1 January 2024, check the current revised text of regulation 4(3) to confirm whether the reference period has been extended. This does not affect the 48-hour figure.

V3. Regulation 5(4). The supplied extract of regulation 5(1) cross-refers to "the requirements of paragraph (4)" but the text of paragraph (4) was not in the material available. Do not paraphrase it; read it from the current revised text before drafting or auditing an opt-out agreement. The record-keeping obligation in regulation 4(2) as amended is quoted and can be relied on as stated.

V4. Section 3 above is drawn from the structure of the Regulations and is marked accordingly: the regulation 19 list of disapplied provisions, the exact scope of regulation 23(b) agreements, the Part III exclusion categories, and the young-worker provision should each be confirmed against the current revised text before being relied on in advice. None of them is part of the answer to either ask; they are supplied only so that the opt-out is not mistaken for the only route out of regulation 4.

V5. This is a general statement of the law of England and Wales and Scotland (regulation 4 is marked E+W+S), not advice on any particular worker, contract or rota. Applying it requires the actual reference period, the actual hours including overtime, and the actual opt-out documentation.

§ 50.19 National primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for ozone.




(a) The level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone (O3) is 0.070 parts per million (ppm), daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter or an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.






(b) The 8-hour primary O3 ambient air quality standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to this part.






(c) The level of the national secondary ambient air quality standard for O3 is 0.070 ppm, daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter or an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.





(d) The 8-hour secondary O3 ambient air quality standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to this part.

verdict.summary:
Governing provision: 40 CFR § 50.19 (current eCFR text; amendment at 80 FR 65452, Oct. 26, 2015).

(1) Level — § 50.19(a): The level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone (O3) is 0.070 ppm, daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to part 50 and designated in accordance with part 53, or by an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53. In ppb this is 70 ppb.

(2) When met at a monitoring site — § 50.19(b): The 8-hour primary O3 ambient air quality standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to part 50. Operationally, compute the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average for each of three years, average those three annual fourth-high values, and compare the result to 0.070 ppm; if the result is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, the site meets the standard, and if it is greater than 0.070 ppm, the site does not meet the standard. The statistic is not a single-day peak and not an average of all daily maxima.

(3) Computation details: Appendix U supplies the data-handling rules for the comparison, including data completeness and truncation. The Appendix U examples in part 50 illustrate truncation of a 3-year average of 0.065666 ppm to 0.065 ppm and a valid design value where average data completeness in the O3 monitoring season is greater than 90% and no single year has less than 75% data completeness. Those details implement the § 50.19(b) test; the regulatory level and comparison remain 0.070 ppm.

(4) Secondary standard: § 50.19(c)-(d) sets the secondary 8-hour O3 standard at the same 0.070 ppm level with the same form. The ask is for the primary standard, so this is noted only to distinguish it.

(5) Scope/limitation: This is the rule from the CFR text. A site-specific determination of met/not met requires applying appendix U to that site's quality-assured monitoring data, including any applicable exceptional-events or data-substitution decisions; without site data, no specific site can be declared to meet or not meet the standard.

results.value: Met when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to part 50

quotes.whole:
§ 211.180 General requirements.




(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch.






(b) Records shall be maintained for all components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling for at least 1 year after the expiration date or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the last lot of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling.






(c) All records required under this part, or copies of such records, shall be readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period at the establishment where the activities described in such records occurred. These records or copies thereof shall be subject to photocopying or other means of reproduction as part of such inspection. Records that can be immediately retrieved from another location by computer or other electronic means shall be considered as meeting the requirements of this paragraph.






(d) Records required under this part may be retained either as original records or as true copies such as photocopies, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproductions of the original records. Where reduction techniques, such as microfilming, are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment shall be readily available.






(e) Written records required by this part shall be maintained so that data therein can be used for evaluating, at least annually, the quality standards of each drug product to determine the need for changes in drug product specifications or manufacturing or control procedures. Written procedures shall be established and followed for such evaluations and shall include provisions for:




(1) A review of a representative number of batches, whether approved or rejected, and, where applicable, records associated with the batch.






(2) A review of complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged drug products, and investigations conducted under § 211.192 for each drug product.







(f) Procedures shall be established to assure that the responsible officials of the firm, if they are not personally involved in or immediately aware of such actions, are notified in writing of any investigations conducted under §§ 211.198, 211.204, or 211.208 of these regulations, any recalls, reports of inspectional observations issued by the Food and Drug Administration, or any regulatory actions relating to good manufacturing practices brought by the Food and Drug Administration.



[43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY AFFAIRS NOTE — 21 CFR 211.180(a) RECORD RETENTION

1. ANSWER (both asks, from the controlling text)

Ask 1 — A production, control, or distribution record required by Part 211 that is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product must be retained for at least 1 YEAR AFTER THE EXPIRATION DATE OF THE BATCH.

Ask 2 — For certain OTC drug products that lack expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under 211.137, the same records must be retained for 3 YEARS AFTER DISTRIBUTION OF THE BATCH.

The two are alternative branches of one sentence in 211.180(a); a given batch falls under one or the other, never both.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim)

21 CFR 211.180(a): 'Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch.'

Source note carried by the section: [43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995].

Verified against, and identical in, all of the following fetched primary/agency sources:
- eCFR current, 21 CFR 211.180 (ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-211/subpart-J/section-211.180; sha256 e2e1b62a1b95)
- eCFR current short path (ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-211.180; sha256 e2e1b62a1b95)
- GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 21 vol. 4, sec. 211-180 XML and PDF (2025-04-01 edition; sha256 920835a3e7c6, 2a47c2e14e42)
- eCFR Part 211 full text (ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-211; sha256 c4e0b31049c9)
The FDA CFR search page (accessdata.fda.gov, fr=211.180) returned only navigation boilerplate and no regulatory text; it was not relied on. No conflict exists among the sources that did return text.

3. ASK 1 — WHAT '1 YEAR' IS MEASURED FROM, AND WHAT IT IS NOT MEASURED FROM

Trigger event: the expiration date of the batch. Retention end date = batch expiration date + 1 year (minimum).

Correction to a common misstatement (this appears in the project's working assumptions and should be struck): the clock does NOT start at batch disposition, QA release, or shipment. Those are different events, and using release as the anchor understates the required period whenever the batch is released before its expiration date — which is always. A firm that keeps batch records '1 year after release' is non-compliant.

Practical consequence: because the expiration date is in the future at the time of release, the effective retention measured from release is (remaining shelf life at release) + 1 year. Example: a batch manufactured 2026-01-15 with a 24-month expiry (2028-01-31) and released 2026-03-01 must be retained at least through 2029-01-31 — i.e., roughly 35 months after release, not 12.

'At least' is a floor, not a target. Longer retention may be required by: firm SOP/quality agreement; the product's own stability program commitments; litigation hold; a pending or reasonably anticipated investigation, complaint, recall, or FDA action; or another Part of Title 21 that applies to the same records (verify applicability before relying on 211.180 alone — e.g., biological products under Part 600, devices under Part 820, foods under Part 117). Where two periods apply, the longer governs.

4. ASK 2 — THE OTC BRANCH AND WHY 3 YEARS RUNS FROM DISTRIBUTION

Condition for the 3-year branch, read literally: the product is an OTC drug product, it LACKS expiration dating, and it lacks it BECAUSE it meets the criteria for exemption under 211.137. All three elements must hold.

Why the anchor changes: with no expiration date there is no date to measure 'expiration + 1 year' from, so the regulation substitutes the last observable event in the batch's life — distribution — and lengthens the period from 1 to 3 years to compensate for the absence of an expiry-based dating horizon. Retention end date = date the batch is distributed + 3 years (minimum).

Consistency check with the rest of the regulation: the 3-year figure is repeated, not contradicted, elsewhere in Part 211 for the same product class — 211.170(b)(3) (reserve samples for an OTC drug product exempt from bearing an expiration date under 211.137: 3 years after the lot or batch is distributed) and 211.170(a)(3) (reserve samples of the active ingredient in such a product: 3 years after distribution of the last lot containing it). Nothing in the fetched text states a period shorter than 3 years for these products.

Boundary case to state explicitly in any SOP: if a product is exempt-eligible but the firm nevertheless prints an expiration date, the 3-year branch does not apply — the product is no longer 'lacking expiration dating', and the 1-year-after-expiration rule governs. Conversely, an OTC product that has an expiration date is always on the 1-year branch.

Cross-reference caveat: the operative exemption criteria live in 211.137 itself (including the enforcement-discretion provision for human OTC drug products at 211.137(h), which turns on the labeling bearing no dosage limitations and on stability for at least 3 years supported by stability data). The 211.137 text was NOT among the fetched passages, so that description is stated from regulatory knowledge and must be confirmed against the current eCFR text of 211.137 before it is quoted in an SOP, a quality agreement, or a regulatory filing. This caveat does not affect the two figures above, which come directly from the fetched 211.180(a) text.

5. WHAT COUNTS AS 'SPECIFICALLY ASSOCIATED WITH A BATCH'

Records that are batch-specific and therefore on the 211.180(a) clock include, at minimum: batch production and control records (211.188); production record review and the associated investigation records (211.192); laboratory control records for testing of the batch, including stability and reserve-sample testing tied to it (211.194); distribution records bearing the lot/control number (211.196); and complaint, returned-goods, salvage, and recall records to the extent they identify or concern that batch.

Records NOT tied to a specific batch fall outside 211.180(a). The nearest express provision is 211.180(b), which sets the same pattern of periods for components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling: at least 1 year after the expiration date, or, for 211.137-exempt OTC products, 3 years after distribution of the LAST lot incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling. Note the anchor for the OTC case is the last using lot, not the individual batch.

Open boundary, flagged rather than answered: master production and control records under 211.186 have no separately stated retention period in 211.180. 211.180(e) requires them to be available for the annual quality review, which implies retention across the review cycle, but the section does not fix a number. Common practice is product life plus the batch retention period; that practice is not a codified figure and should not be presented as one. If a specific answer is needed for master records, it requires a separate analysis (and possibly an FDA inquiry or reliance on 211.180(c) availability obligations).

6. OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS THAT TRAVEL WITH THE PERIODS (do not change the figures; do change whether the records are usable)

- 211.180(c): during the retention period the records, or copies, must be readily available for authorized inspection at the establishment where the recorded activities occurred. Records immediately retrievable from another location by computer or other electronic means satisfy this. Off-site archive with a retrieval lead time that is not 'immediate' does not.
- 211.180(d): original records or true copies (photocopy, microfilm/microfiche, or other accurate reproduction) are acceptable; where reduction techniques are used, reader and photocopying equipment must be readily available.
- 211.180(e): written records must be maintained so the data can be used for the annual quality-standard evaluation, including review of a representative number of batches (approved and rejected) and of complaints, recalls, returned/salvaged product, and 211.192 investigations.
- Electronic records/signatures: if the retained record is electronic, Part 11 applies in addition (verify scope before assuming exemptions).

7. RETENTION-MATRIX RULE (drop-in logic for a records retention schedule)

For each record, resolve in this order:
  Step 1 — Is the record required by Part 211 and specifically associated with a batch?
      No  -> apply 211.180(b) if it concerns components/containers/closures/labeling (1 yr after expiry, or 3 yrs after distribution of the last using lot for 211.137-exempt OTC); otherwise apply the governing section or firm policy, and escalate if none exists.
      Yes -> Step 2.
  Step 2 — Does the batch bear an expiration date?
      Yes -> retain through (expiration date + 1 year).
      No, and the product is an OTC drug product exempt from expiration dating under 211.137 -> retain through (date of distribution of the batch + 3 years).
      No, and no 211.137 exemption basis is documented -> compliance gap; the 3-year branch is not available on these facts. Escalate.
  Step 3 — Compare with any longer period required by SOP, quality agreement, other applicable Parts of Title 21, or a hold (litigation, recall, investigation). Retain to the LATEST date.
  Step 4 — Record the computed destruction-eligible date and the basis (the specific citation) in the retention schedule; do not destroy on the basis of release date or file-closure date.

8. COMMON ERRORS THIS NOTE IS WRITTEN TO PREVENT

(a) Measuring the 1 year from disposition or release instead of from the expiration date — the most frequent error and the one embedded in the project's working assumption.
(b) Applying the 3-year OTC period to an OTC product that carries an expiration date.
(c) Applying the 3-year OTC period to a prescription product, or to an OTC product with no documented 211.137 exemption basis.
(d) Measuring the OTC 3 years from manufacture or release rather than from distribution.
(e) Treating 'at least' as an exact period and destroying records the moment the minimum elapses, ignoring holds and longer applicable periods.
(f) Conflating 211.180(a) batch records with 211.180(b) component/container/closure/labeling records, which are anchored to the last using lot.
(g) Relying on a pre-1995 version of the section; the OTC clause is part of the text as amended at 60 FR 4091 (Jan. 20, 1995).

9. AMENDMENT STATUS

211.180(a) is unchanged in the current text from the version carrying the 1995 amendment citation; no later amendment to 211.180(a) appears in any fetched source. The 2024 amendment at 89 FR 51770 (June 18, 2024, effective Dec. 18, 2025) touched 211.170 (reserve samples) and does not alter the 211.180(a) periods; it does not change the 3-year figure cited in section 4, which is corroborated by the amended 211.170(b)(3) text. The section as printed in the 2025-04-01 CFR edition matches the current eCFR text, so no version question arises for the two figures requested.

10. SOURCE-VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THIS IS QUOTED IN AN SOP OR FILING

Confirm the two figures against the current eCFR text of 211.180(a) on the date of use (the text is stable but the citation must be current); confirm the text of 211.137, in particular the OTC provision at 211.137(h), which was not in the fetched set; confirm whether any FDA guidance or warning letter has taken an enforcement position on retention for 211.137-exempt OTC products that differs from the plain text (none was identified in the fetched material); and confirm no other Part of Title 21 applicable to the specific product imposes a longer period.

§ 825.220 Protection for employees who request leave or otherwise assert FMLA rights.
(a) The FMLA prohibits interference with an employee's rights under the law, and with legal proceedings or inquiries relating to an employee's rights. More specifically, the law contains the following employee protections:
(1) An employer is prohibited from interfering with, restraining, or denying the exercise of (or attempts to exercise) any rights provided by the Act.
(2) An employer is prohibited from discharging or in any other way discriminating against any person (whether or not an employee) for opposing or complaining about any unlawful practice under the Act.
(3) All persons (whether or not employers) are prohibited from discharging or in any other way discriminating against any person (whether or not an employee) because that person has—
(i) Filed any charge, or has instituted (or caused to be instituted) any proceeding under or related to this Act;
(ii) Given, or is about to give, any information in connection with an inquiry or proceeding relating to a right under this Act;
(iii) Testified, or is about to testify, in any inquiry or proceeding relating to a right under this Act.

verdict.summary:
MEMORANDUM — FMLA ENTITLEMENT UNDER 29 CFR § 825.200(a) (EXCLUDING COVERED-SERVICEMEMBER CAREGIVER LEAVE)

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
Under 29 CFR § 825.200(a), how much FMLA leave is an eligible employee entitled to, and over what period is that entitlement measured, leaving aside leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness?

2. SHORT ANSWER
(a) Amount: 12 workweeks. (b) Period: during any 12-month period, the method for defining which 12-month period being chosen by the employer from the four options in § 825.200(b). The 12 workweeks is a single combined ceiling for all five qualifying reasons listed in § 825.200(a)(1)-(5), not 12 workweeks per reason.

3. CONTROLLING TEXT (29 CFR § 825.200(a), as published; verified against eCFR and the 2025 govinfo CFR compilation)
"(a) Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons:
(1) The birth of the employee's son or daughter, and to care for the newborn child;
(2) The placement with the employee of a son or daughter for adoption or foster care, and to care for the newly placed child;
(3) To care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition;
(4) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform one or more of the essential functions of his or her job; and,
(5) Because of any qualifying exigency arising out of the fact that the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent is a military member on covered active duty status (or has been notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty)."

4. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT READING (the operative phrases)
4.1 "an eligible employee" — the entitlement is stated for an employee who satisfies the eligibility definition in Part 825 (see § 825.110: employed for at least 12 months, at least 1,250 hours of service in the preceding 12 months, and employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed within 75 miles). This memorandum assumes eligibility and does not re-derive it; the amount and period stated here are the entitlement once eligibility is established.
4.2 "is limited to a total of 12 workweeks" — the unit is the workweek, not the calendar week and not the pay period. The ceiling is a "total," i.e., an aggregate across all reasons in (a)(1)-(5), not a per-reason allocation. Practically: an employee who takes 4 workweeks for the birth of a child, 3 workweeks for the employee's own serious health condition, and 2 workweeks of qualifying exigency leave has used 9 of the same 12 workweeks and has 3 remaining in the applicable 12-month period.
4.3 "of leave during any 12-month period" — the 12 workweeks is measured against a 12-month measuring period, defined by the employer's choice of method under § 825.200(b) (see section 5). "Any" signals that the regulation does not fix one calendar anchor; it fixes a length (12 months) and leaves the anchor to the employer.
4.4 "for any one, or more, of the following reasons" — reasons (a)(1)-(5) are alternatives that draw on the same single bank of 12 workweeks. They do not stack.
4.5 Reason (a)(5) in particular: qualifying exigency leave (arising from a family member's covered active duty status or notification of an impending call or order to covered active duty) is expressly one of the (a) reasons. It therefore falls inside the 12 workweeks and does not add to them.
4.6 The opening clause, "Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness" — this carve-out is the constraint imposed on this analysis. The 26-workweek military caregiver entitlement in § 825.200(f) and the combined 26-workweek cap in § 825.200(g) (both keyed to § 825.127(e)) are outside the scope of this answer and are not added to, netted against, or otherwise combined with the 12 workweeks stated here. Nothing in this memorandum should be read as stating an entitlement above 12 workweeks for the reasons in (a)(1)-(5).

5. THE MEASUREMENT PERIOD — § 825.200(b) VERBATIM
"(b) An employer is permitted to choose any one of the following methods for determining the 12-month period in which the 12 weeks of leave entitlement described in paragraph (a) of this section occurs:
(1) The calendar year;
(2) Any fixed 12-month leave year, such as a fiscal year, a year required by State law, or a year starting on an employee's anniversary date;
(3) The 12-month period measured forward from the date any employee's first FMLA leave under paragraph (a) begins; or,
(4) A 'rolling' 12-month period measured backward from the date an employee uses any FMLA leave as described in paragraph (a)."

Operational translation of each method (for applying the 12-workweek cap):
- Method (1), calendar year: the bank resets on January 1; leave taken in the current calendar year counts against that year's 12 workweeks.
- Method (2), fixed 12-month leave year: the bank resets on a fixed date the employer designates (fiscal year, State-law year, anniversary date); each designated year carries its own 12 workweeks.
- Method (3), forward from first leave: the 12-month clock starts on the date the employee first takes FMLA leave under (a); the 12 workweeks is available for the 12 months following that date, and a new period begins when the next first-use date occurs after the prior period ends.
- Method (4), rolling backward: for each date the employee uses FMLA leave, look back 12 months from that date; the employee may use only the balance of 12 workweeks not already used in that trailing 12-month window.

Worked arithmetic for the rolling-backward method (method (4)), to show the cap is never exceeded: employee used 3 workweeks in March and 2 workweeks in August of the same year. In November the employee requests 8 more workweeks. Looking back 12 months from each November date on which leave would be used, the 5 workweeks already used remain inside the window, so the available balance is 12 - 5 = 7 workweeks, not 8. The request must be reduced to 7 workweeks (or the excess treated as non-FMLA) to stay within the § 825.200(a) ceiling.

6. WHAT THE ANSWER IS NOT
- It is not 12 workweeks per qualifying event or per reason. (a) says "a total of 12 workweeks ... for any one, or more" reasons.
- It is not 12 workweeks plus 12 workweeks for qualifying exigency leave. Exigency leave is reason (a)(5), inside the 12.
- It is not 26 workweeks. The 26-workweek figures appear only in § 825.200(f) and (g), which govern covered-servicemember caregiver leave and are expressly excluded here.
- It is not a calendar year by force of law. The calendar year is only one of four permissible employer choices under (b).

7. CROSS-REFERENCES AND DEFINITIONS TO CONFIRM WHEN APPLYING THE ANSWER
- "Eligible employee": Part 825 eligibility provisions (see § 825.110).
- "Spouse, son, daughter, parent," "serious health condition," "covered active duty status," "qualifying exigency," "covered servicemember": defined elsewhere in Part 825 (e.g., §§ 825.102, 825.113, 825.126, 825.127). These definitions determine whether a given absence draws on the 12 workweeks; they do not change the amount or the period.
- § 825.200(c)-(e): these paragraphs were not among the passages retrieved for this analysis and are not quoted or paraphrased here. They address administration of the (b) method choice (consistency of application, default where no method is selected, and changing methods). Confirm their current text before advising on method selection or method changes; nothing in the amount or period stated above depends on them.
- § 825.802: special calculation rule for airline flight crew employees (72 days in lieu of 12 workweeks; 156 days for military caregiver leave). This is a separate, occupation-specific rule outside § 825.200(a) and does not alter the figure stated here for the general workforce. Flag it only if the employee is airline flight crew.

8. ONE-LINE HOLDING
Under 29 CFR § 825.200(a), an eligible employee is entitled to a total of 12 workweeks of FMLA leave during any 12-month period, for any one or more of the five listed reasons (birth/care of newborn; placement/care of newly placed child; care of a family member with a serious health condition; the employee's own serious health condition; qualifying exigency arising from a family member's covered active duty), with the 12-month period defined by the employer's choice among the four methods in § 825.200(b) — and excluding, per the constraint on this request, the separate 26-workweek covered-servicemember caregiver entitlement.

Abstract
This guideline focuses on the authentication of subjects who interact with government information systems over networks to establish that a given claimant is a subscriber who has been previously authenticated. The result of the authentication process may be used locally by the system performing the authentication or asserted elsewhere in a federated identity system. This document defines technical requirements for each of the three authenticator assurance levels. The guidelines are not intended to constrain the development or use of standards outside of this purpose. This publication supersedes NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-63B.

Strength of Passwords
This appendix is informative.
This appendix uses the word “password” for ease of discussion. Where used, it should be interpreted to include passphrases and PINs.
Introduction
Passwords are a widely used form of authentication despite concerns about their use from both a usability and security standpoint [Persistence]. Humans have a limited ability to memorize complex, arbitrary secrets, so they often choose passwords that can be easily guessed. To address the resultant security concerns, online services have introduced rules that increase the effective strength of these passwords. The most notable form is composition rules, which require users to choose passwords that are constructed using a mix of character types (e.g., at least one digit, uppercase letter, and symbol). However, analyses of breached password databases reveal that the benefit of such rules is less significant than initially thought [Policies], and the impacts on usability and memorability are severe.

Central vs. Local Verification
While passwords that are used as a separate authentication factor are often centrally verified by the CSP’s verifier, those that are used as an activation factor for a multi-factor authenticator are either verified locally by the authenticator or used to derive the authenticator output, which will be incorrect if the wrong activation factor is used. The attack surfaces and vulnerabilities for central and local verification are very different. Accordingly, the requirements for centrally verified passwords differ from those verified locally. Centrally verified passwords require the verifier (i.e., an online resource) to store salted and iteratively hashed verification secrets for all of the subscribers’ passwords. Although the salting and hashing process increases the computational effort to determine the passwords from the hashes, the verifier is an attractive target for attackers, particularly those interested in compromising an arbitrary subscriber rather than a specific one.

Abstract
This guideline focuses on the authentication of subjects who interact with government information systems over networks to establish that a given claimant is a subscriber who has been previously authenticated. The result of the authentication process may be used locally by the system performing the authentication or asserted elsewhere in a federated identity system. This document defines technical requirements for each of the three authenticator assurance levels. The guidelines are not intended to constrain the development or use of standards outside of this purpose. This publication supersedes NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-63B.

verdict.summary:
SECURITY ENGINEERING NOTE — Password length requirements in NIST SP 800-63B-4

AUTHORITATIVE SOURCE
NIST Special Publication 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, final, published July 2025, DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63B-4, https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/63/b/4/final. It supersedes SP 800-63B (03/02/2020). The controlling clause is the 'Password Verifiers' requirement list in Sec. 3.1.1.2 (rendered as the 'Password Verifiers' subsection of Sec. 3.1.1 in the HTML edition at https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/).

THE THREE VALUES

1) Password used as a single-factor authentication mechanism — minimum 15 characters.
   Verbatim: 'Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length.'
   This is a SHALL: a hard requirement on the verifier and CSP, not a recommendation. It is the floor for a password that is, by itself, the authentication factor (i.e., single-factor / 1FA password authentication).

2) Password used only as part of multi-factor authentication — minimum 8 characters.
   Verbatim: 'Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length.'
   The 'MAY be shorter' is permission to go below 15; the 'SHALL require ... a minimum of eight characters' is the hard floor. The relaxation is conditional on the password being used only as a component of MFA — if the same credential can also be used alone, the 15-character floor governs. The appendix (App. A, 'Strength of Passwords', A.4 Central vs. Local Verification) explains the rationale: for activation factors verified locally, threats are less dependent on password length and complexity, so requirements are relaxed relative to centrally verified passwords.

3) Maximum length the verifier should permit — at least 64 characters.
   Verbatim: 'Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters.'
   Read precisely: the verifier's accepted maximum must be no lower than 64 characters. 64 is a floor on the ceiling, not a cap. It is a SHOULD, but treating it as a MUST is the safe engineering posture; refusing long passwords or silently truncating at 64 is the failure mode the clause exists to prevent.

VERSION DISAMBIGUATION (material — do not mix revisions)
The withdrawn 2nd public draft, NIST SP 800-63B-4 2pd (August 2024; withdrawn 2025-08-01), carried a single combined clause: 'Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords to be a minimum of eight characters in length and SHOULD require passwords to be a minimum of 15 characters in length.' That draft does not distinguish single-factor from MFA use, so it cannot produce the 15/8 split asked for here. Any answer attributing 15/8 to '800-63B-4' must be attributed to the July 2025 final, not the 2pd draft. For contrast, SP 800-63B (2020) required a minimum of 8 characters and SHOULD permit at least 64; the final -4 raises the single-factor floor to a mandatory 15.

SUPPORTING NORMATIVE CONTEXT (same clause, needed to implement the lengths correctly)
- Character counting: 'Each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character when evaluating password length.' Length is measured in Unicode code points, not bytes and not UTF-16 code units. A 15-character minimum means 15 code points.
- Accepted character set: verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept all printing ASCII (RFC 20) characters plus the space character, and SHOULD accept Unicode (ISO/IEC 10646) characters. A length policy that silently rejects non-ASCII or spaces can make the minimum unmeetable for legitimate subscribers.
- Composition: verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., character-class mixing). Length plus blocklist screening is the intended control; do not add complexity rules on top of these minima.
- Expiration: verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require periodic password change; force a change only on evidence of authenticator compromise.
- Mistyping allowances (e.g., trimming leading/trailing whitespace, case-folding the leading character) are permitted only if the password remains at least the required minimum length after such processing — so apply the 15/8 check post-normalization, and only normalize in ways that do not reduce length below the floor.
- Assurance levels: the password-length requirement in the final is stated uniformly, not varied by AAL. Practically, a password alone cannot satisfy AAL2 or AAL3 (both require MFA), so single-factor password authentication is an AAL1 construct; the 8-character floor is the one that applies to password components inside AAL2/AAL3 multi-factor authentication. Apply the higher floor whenever the credential could be used standalone.

IMPLEMENTATION CHECKLIST (verifier configuration)
1. Enforce minLength = 15 for any password credential usable as a sole factor; enforce minLength = 8 only where the credential is provably MFA-only and cannot be used standalone.
2. Set maxLength >= 64 (recommend 64 or higher, effectively unbounded) and never truncate input before hashing/verification. Truncation is a silent violation of the SHOULD and destroys entropy.
3. Count length in Unicode code points; validate after any whitespace/case normalization and reject if the post-normalization length falls below the applicable floor.
4. Do not add composition rules; do not add forced rotation; do add blocklist screening per the same section.
5. Record which floor applies as an attribute of the credential type, not as a global setting, so an MFA-only activation secret cannot be reused as a standalone password at 8 characters.

BOTTOM LINE
Single-factor password: 15 characters minimum (SHALL). Password used only within MFA: 8 characters minimum (SHALL), with shortening below 15 permitted (MAY). Maximum accepted length: at least 64 characters (SHOULD). All three from NIST SP 800-63B-4 (final, July 2025), Sec. 3.1.1.2 Password Verifiers.

verdict.summary:
# RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1 — Maximum SMTP Line Lengths

## 1. Answer

| Object | Section | Maximum total length | What the count covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Text line** (a line inside DATA) | §4.5.3.1.6 | **1000 octets** | The entire line **including the trailing `<CRLF>`**, **not counting** the leading dot duplicated for transparency |
| **Reply line** (one line of a server reply) | §4.5.3.1.5 | **512 octets** | The **3-digit reply code**, the separator (`-` or `<SP>`), the text, **and the trailing `<CRLF>`** |
| *(Command line — included because "SMTP text line" is ambiguous)* | §4.5.3.1.4 | **512 octets** | The **command word**, the SP and arguments/parameters, **and the trailing `<CRLF>`** |

Unit is **octets (8-bit bytes)**, not characters. Both 512 limits and the 1000 limit are **minimum maxima**: every implementation MUST be able to receive objects at least that large, and MAY accept larger. Both RFC texts add that SMTP extensions may raise the limits.

## 2. Source text (verbatim)

> **4.5.3.1.4. Command Line**
> The maximum total length of a command line including the command word and the `<CRLF>` is 512 octets. SMTP extensions may be used to increase this limit.
>
> **4.5.3.1.5. Reply Line**
> The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and the `<CRLF>` is 512 octets. More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies.
>
> **4.5.3.1.6. Text Line**
> The maximum total length of a text line including the `<CRLF>` is 1000 octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency). This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions.

Preceded in §4.5.3.1 by the statement that lengths are expressed *"in octets where absolute lengths, rather than character counts, are intended."* These figures are identical across the three independently fetched copies (rfc-editor.org HTML, datatracker.ietf.org, xmox.nl) — sha256 `5df422fb9940`, `842bce344af6`, `0919e1c1667e` respectively. No erratum altering these two figures appears in the fetched material; verify at `rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc5321` before freezing them into a code comment.

## 3. Disambiguating "SMTP text line"

RFC 5321 uses three distinct terms and they must not be conflated:

- **Text line** (§4.5.3.1.6) = a line of message content inside DATA. **1000 octets incl. CRLF.**
- **Command line** (§4.5.3.1.4) = one client command. **512 octets incl. CRLF.**
- **Reply line** (§4.5.3.1.5) = one line of a server response. **512 octets incl. CRLF.**

If the question means "a line of text sent as a command", the answer is 512. If it means the §4.5.3.1.6 object literally named "Text Line", the answer is 1000. The reply-line figure is 512 either way.

## 4. Octet budget — what exactly fits inside each limit

```
CONSTANTS (RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1)
  CRLF                     = 2 octets
  Reply-code               = 3 octets (%x32-35 %x30-35 %x30-39 => 200-599)
  Reply separator          = 1 octet  ('-' intermediate, <SP> final)

DERIVED MAXIMA
  Reply line total         = 512
    -> max textstring      = 512 - 3 - 1 - 2 = 506 octets   (separator present)
    -> bare-code line      = 512 - 3 - 2     = 510 octets   (no text; SP omitted)
  Command line total       = 512
    -> max arguments       = 512 - len(verb) - 1 (SP) - 2 (CRLF)
                            = 509 - len(verb)
       verb "MAIL" (4)     -> 505 argument octets
       verb "RCPT" (4)     -> 505 argument octets
       verb "EHLO" (4)     -> 505 argument octets
  Text line total          = 1000
    -> max content         = 1000 - 2 = 998 octets
    -> dot-stuffed on wire = 998 + 1 (transparency dot) + 2 (CRLF) = 1001 octets
       but the DEFINED count is still 1000: the duplicated dot is excluded.
```

**Included in the counts** (all of it, with nothing added later):

- Text line: every content octet, the terminating `<CR>` and `<LF>`. Excluded: the transparency dot prepended to a line beginning with `.`; the `.` `<CRLF>` end-of-data terminator is not a text line at all.
- Reply line: the three reply-code digits, the `-` or `<SP>` separator, the textstring, and `<CR>` `<LF>`. Each line of a multiline reply is measured **individually** against 512; the multiline reply as a whole has no total limit. Note RFC 5321 §4.1.1: *"The space (blank) following the reply code is considered part of the text"* — so the separator octet is inside the 506-octet text budget as well as inside the 512 total.
- Command line: the verb, the separating SP, every argument octet including `FROM:`/`TO:` and the `<...>` path punctuation, every ESMTP parameter, and `<CR>` `<LF>`. Pipelined commands are counted one line at a time.

**Not included:** any octet of a preceding or following line; the dot-stuffing octet; the DATA terminator.

## 5. Consistency with the other §4.5.3.1 limits

| Object | Limit | Worst-case line construction | Total | Fits? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reverse/forward-path | 256 | `MAIL FROM:<` + 256 + `>` + CRLF = 4+1+5+256+2 | 268 | yes (244 spare) |
| reverse/forward-path | 256 | `RCPT TO:<` + 256 + `>` + CRLF = 4+1+3+256+2 | 266 | yes (246 spare) |
| domain | 255 | `EHLO ` + 255 + CRLF = 4+1+255+2 | 262 | yes (250 spare) |
| local-part | 64 | consumed inside the path budget above | — | yes |

The 512-octet command limit is therefore never the binding constraint for a bare-path command; it binds only when ESMTP parameters are appended (e.g. `SIZE=`, `AUTH=`, `BODY=8BITMIME`), and that slack is exactly 244/246 octets.

## 6. Implementation rules

### 6.1 Server — reading a command line

```go
const (
	MaxCommandLineOctets = 512  // RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.4, CRLF included
	MaxTextLineOctets    = 1000 // RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.6, CRLF included, dot excluded
)

var ErrLineTooLong = errors.New("line too long")

// readLine returns the line INCLUDING its CRLF. max counts the CRLF.
func readLine(r *bufio.Reader, max int) ([]byte, error) {
	buf := make([]byte, 0, 128)
	for {
		b, err := r.ReadByte()
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		buf = append(buf, b)
		if len(buf) > max {
			// RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.4: do not crash. Drain to end of line to resync,
			// then let the caller emit "500 5.5.2 Line too long".
			for b != '\n' {
				if b, err = r.ReadByte(); err != nil {
					return nil, err
				}
			}
			return nil, ErrLineTooLong
		}
		if n := len(buf); n >= 2 && buf[n-2] == '\r' && buf[n-1] == '\n' {
			return buf, nil
		}
	}
}
```

Rules for the server:

1. Accept a command line of **exactly 512** octets. Reject at **513**. Off-by-one here is the classic bug: the limit includes CRLF, so the check is `len > 512`, not `len >= 512`.
2. On overflow, reply `500 5.5.2 Line too long` and keep the session alive; do not drop the connection, and do not parse the truncated fragment.
3. Be liberal on input: tolerate a bare `<LF>` (1 octet terminator) even though the count is defined against `<CRLF>`, and count what was actually received.
4. Enforce 1000 octets per DATA line **after** transparency-dot removal, i.e. count the line as the sender's content plus CRLF. The dot-stuffed wire form may legitimately be 1001 octets.
5. An overlong DATA line has no mandated reply code in §4.5.3.1; the common practice is `500 5.5.2 Line too long` at end of DATA or acceptance with truncation. Whatever the policy, it must be applied consistently and logged.

### 6.2 Server — emitting a reply line

```go
const (
	MaxReplyLineOctets = 512 // RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.5, code + separator + text + CRLF
	ReplyCodeLen       = 3
	ReplySepLen        = 1
	CRLFLen            = 2
	MaxReplyTextOctets = MaxReplyLineOctets - ReplyCodeLen - ReplySepLen - CRLFLen // = 506
)

// writeReply renders text as a (possibly multiline) reply. Every rendered line
// is <= 512 octets including code, separator and CRLF.
func writeReply(w io.Writer, code int, text string) error {
	chunks := splitText(text, MaxReplyTextOctets) // each <= 506 octets
	if len(chunks) == 0 {
		chunks = []string{""}
	}
	for i, c := range chunks {
		sep := "-"
		if i == len(chunks)-1 {
			sep = " "
		}
		line := fmt.Sprintf("%03d%s%s\r\n", code, sep, c)
		if len(line) > MaxReplyLineOctets {
			return fmt.Errorf("reply line %d octets exceeds %d", len(line), MaxReplyLineOctets)
		}
		if _, err := io.WriteString(w, line); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}
	return nil
}
```

Rules for the server:

1. Never emit a reply line longer than 512 octets. If human-readable text is longer, **split into a multiline reply** — that is precisely what §4.5.3.1.5 means by "More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies."
2. Every line of a multiline reply carries the **same** reply code (§4.1.1); only the separator differs (`-` on all but the last, `<SP>` on the last).
3. Split on octet boundaries at whitespace where possible. Base reply text is `HT / SP / Printable US-ASCII` only, so multi-byte sequences are not a concern in base SMTP; if a private extension emits UTF-8 in reply text, never split inside a multi-byte sequence.
4. Keep the `<SP>` on the final line even when it carries no text; clients MUST tolerate its absence, but servers SHOULD send it.
5. Do not count the CRLF of one line against another: the 512 budget is per line, and a 20-line reply is legal at 20 × 512.

### 6.3 Client

- Buffer and accept at least 512 octets per reply line; a client that caps at 510 truncates valid replies.
- For interoperation with non-conforming servers, read with a generous hard cap (e.g. 4096 octets) and truncate for display rather than aborting; but never *require* more than 512.
- Determine the action from the 3-digit code only, not the text (§4.1.1).
- When constructing commands, budget to 512 octets and fail locally with a clear error rather than emitting an overlong line the server will reject with 500.
- When sending DATA, wrap content at 998 octets before dot-stuffing; wrapping after dot-stuffing produces 997-octet content lines and needless rewrites.

## 7. Extension interactions (why "maximum" is conditional)

- **§4.5.3.1.4 / §4.5.3.1.6 both say the limit may be raised by an SMTP service extension.** The 512/1000 figures are the guaranteed floor of the maximum, not an absolute ceiling.
- **AUTH (RFC 4954)** is the canonical case of a command line exceeding 512 octets because of a long base64 initial response; implementations must consult that specification for the increased bound rather than assuming 512.
- **SIZE (RFC 1870)** governs *message content* (§4.5.3.1.7, ≥ 64K), not line length. Do not confuse the two.
- **SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531)** does **not** raise the 512/1000 octet limits. It permits UTF-8 in envelope addresses, so a local-part or domain expressed in multi-byte characters consumes the same 64/255/256/512 octet budgets faster and holds fewer characters. Any code that counts characters instead of octets will overrun the limit under SMTPUTF8.
- **LIMITS (draft-freed-smtp-limits)** is an Internet-Draft referenced in the IETF EMAILCORE review of §4.5.3.1 (G.7.8, "Review different size limits"). It is not authoritative today; treat 512/1000 as binding until an RFC is published.

## 8. Verification test vectors

| # | Case | Bytes | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Command line, exactly 512 octets incl. CRLF | 512 | accepted |
| 2 | Command line, 513 octets incl. CRLF | 513 | `500 5.5.2 Line too long`, session survives |
| 3 | `MAIL FROM:<` + 256-octet path + `>` + CRLF | 268 | accepted |
| 4 | `RCPT TO:<` + 256-octet path + `>` + CRLF | 266 | accepted |
| 5 | `EHLO ` + 255-octet domain + CRLF | 262 | accepted |
| 6 | Reply line, code + `-` + 506-octet text + CRLF | 512 | emitted as-is |
| 7 | Reply line, code + `-` + 507-octet text + CRLF | 513 | split into 2 lines, each ≤ 512 |
| 8 | Reply, bare code + CRLF | 5 | accepted by client (SP omitted) |
| 9 | DATA line, 998 content octets + CRLF | 1000 | accepted |
| 10 | DATA line, 999 content octets + CRLF | 1001 | over limit — apply documented policy |
| 11 | DATA line beginning with `.`, 998 content octets, dot-stuffed + CRLF | 1001 on wire / 1000 as defined | **accepted** — the duplicated dot is excluded from the count |
| 12 | 20-line multiline reply, each line 512 octets | 20 × 512 | accepted; no aggregate limit |

Case 11 is the one that catches naive implementations: a receiver that enforces `len(wire_line) <= 1000` rejects a legal maximum-length line.

## 9. One-line summary for code comments

> RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1: text (DATA) line ≤ 1000 octets **including CRLF**, excluding the duplicated transparency dot; reply line ≤ 512 octets **including the 3-digit code, the `-`/SP separator, the text, and CRLF**; command line ≤ 512 octets **including the command word, all arguments, and CRLF**. All counts are octets. Extensions may raise them.

complete text must be marked so the SMTP client knows when it can
stop reading the reply.  This requires a special format to indicate a
multiple line reply.

4.5.3.1.1.  Local-part
The maximum total length of a user name or other local-part is 64
octets.
4.5.3.1.2.  Domain
The maximum total length of a domain name or number is 255 octets.
4.5.3.1.3.  Path
The maximum total length of a reverse-path or forward-path is 256
octets (including the punctuation and element separators).
4.5.3.1.4.  Command Line
The maximum total length of a command line including the command word
and the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  SMTP extensions may be used to
increase this limit.
